rows.design: [within-subject split-forearm comparison: tretinoin on one dorsal forearm, Nivea cream on both; no other control]; randomisation of side, blinding and assessor not reported
rows.skin_tone: not reported for the four treated women [the separate 40-woman epidemiology sample was 'Caucasian women (phototypes 2 and 3)'; whether the treated women came from it is not stated]
rows.patients_enrolled: not reported (the paper states only how many completed)

rows.diagnosis: mixed: IGH and macular hypomelanosis (MH) of photodamaged skin, results pooled; 1 of four treated women had IGH, three had MH
rows.lesions_enrolled: not reported ('selected macules'; count not stated)
rows.analysis_unit: lesion [results are described for 'tretinoin-treated macules' without counts; statistical unit not reported]
rows.intervention: topical tretinoin cream (Retin-A) once nightly on one dorsal forearm: 0.025% for 1 week, 0.05% the second week, then 0.1% to the end of a 4-month course; Nivea cream each morning on both forearms; no sunscreen (fall and winter, long sleeves)
rows.comparator: contralateral dorsal forearm, Nivea cream only (see the Nivea row)
rows.endpoint_definition: not reported as a defined scale: clinical appearance of the macules and repigmentation on UVA and epiluminescence photographs, described qualitatively
rows.assessment_method: clinical photographs, UVA photography, parallel-polarized photography and epiluminescence photography before and after treatment; assessor and grading not reported
rows.time_from_start: after 4 months of nightly treatment; 'great improvement' already evident after 2 months
rows.time_from_last_treatment: NOT_DERIVABLE: assessed 'after treatment' / 'after 4 months'; the interval between the last application and the assessment is not reported [presumably at the end of treatment]
rows.arm_result: tretinoin-treated macules 'clinically disappeared after 4 months' with 'partial repigmentation' on UVA and epiluminescence photos, in both IGH and MH (pooled; no proportion or lesion count reported)
rows.complete_match: not reported [the macules are said to have 'clinically disappeared', but pigmentation is described as only partial; no colour match to surrounding skin is stated]
rows.dark_overshoot: not reported [no darkening beyond the surrounding skin described]; the surrounding skin showed a decrease in pigmentation
rows.texture_or_scar: almost complete recovery of glyphics; in the elasticity subset (3 subjects, IGH and MH pooled) distensibility R0 rose 77% and gross elasticity R2 34% versus pretreatment (p<0.005); R0 and R2 higher than on Nivea-treated macules (p<0.05); acanthosis with correction of atypia on histology
rows.uncertainty: Very small study: four treated women, of whom only 1 had IGH (3 had macular hypomelanosis, MH). Clinical, photographic and elasticity results are reported pooled for IGH and MH, never per lesion type or per lesion, and with no lesion counts, no repigmentation scale, no grading criteria and no named or blinded assessor. The Results say the treated macules 'clinically disappeared' yet also report only 'partial repigmentation' (abstract: 'a partial restoration of pigmentation'); the Fig. 2 caption (IGH) says 'recovery of pigmentation'. Read here as partial repigmentation, not complete coverage or colour match. The surrounding skin 'showed a decrease in pigmentation' after tretinoin, so part of the reduced contrast may come from the surrounding skin lightening, not the macule darkening [inference]; the study ran in fall and winter without sunscreen, which may also lower surrounding pigment [inference]. Allocation of the tretinoin side is not described. The authors themselves write that 'maintenance therapy may be required for durable effects'. Elasticity was measured in only 3 subjects; which lesion types they had is not stated.
